item.title: Reducing Administrative Burdens: Strategies, Stakeholders, and Impact
item.content:encoded:
Matthias Döring, University of Southern Denmark

Ayesha Masood, Lahore University of Management Sciences

Johan Sandén, Södertörn University

Administrative burdens—the learning, compliance, and psychological costs citizens face when interacting with government—have become a significant research area. These burdens disproportionately affect vulnerable groups and threaten administrative equity, particularly in welfare systems. Scholars are increasingly investigating strategies to reduce or mitigate these burdens, including fostering citizen resources through intermediaries and improving organizational design and communication practices.

This special issue seeks contributions examining burden-reduction initiatives undertaken by various actors across different contexts and levels of governance. It welcomes research investigating how public organizations, managers, and street-level bureaucrats can reduce administrative burdens, which interventions are effective, whether they benefit all groups equally, and how burden-reduction efforts are perceived within public administration. The issue aims to generate societal impact by addressing challenges relevant to practitioners and policymakers working to reduce administrative burdens.

Appel publié par International Journal of Public Sector Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Digital initiatives to reduce burdens, including algorithms, automation, and AI
  • How burden-reduction initiatives are initiated and defined - and by whom
  • Initiatives aimed at preventing administrative limbo or repeated referrals
  • How do different public organizations react to and enact burden reduction strategies across policy sectors?
  • How do street-level bureaucrats perceive, avoid, or create burden reduction strategies?
  • How do different types of intermediaries (private companies vs. NGOs vs. public intermediaries) support citizens in their attempt to overcome burdens?
  • The relationship between burden-reduction interventions and social inequalities
  • What is the relationship between leadership and the responsiveness to burden reduction strategies?
  • The interplay between bureaucratization and administrative processes in producing burdens
  • How do administrative reforms affect administrative burden?
  • Which role do burden reduction strategies play in the political debate? Is there a connection to political action?
  • The materiality of burden reduction, administrative burdens, and responses.

Timeline

  • October 31, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • February 28, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Arts Organizations and Street-Level Bureaucracy
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Paquette, University of Ottawa

Street-level bureaucracy, a concept developed to describe how front-line professionals implement public policies through discretionary decision-making, remains highly relevant to contemporary policy studies across multiple sectors. The special issue seeks to extend this framework to arts and heritage organizations, an area where street-level bureaucracy has received limited scholarly attention despite growing evidence that cultural professionals operate as street-level bureaucrats navigating policy implementation, resource constraints, and complex social mandates.

The call invites manuscripts examining how arts professionals engage with street-level bureaucracy, particularly focusing on care work dimensions as cultural organizations increasingly participate in social cohesion and vulnerability integration initiatives. Submissions should explore the creative strategies, routines, and coping mechanisms that cultural professionals develop, and analyze how the street-level bureaucracy concept illuminates arts management across varied global contexts.

Appel publié par The Journal of Arts Management, Law, and Society. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Street-level bureaucracy and care work in arts and heritage organizations
  • Work, routines and coping mechanisms in cultural organizations
  • Conceptual analysis of street-level bureaucracy in arts management
  • How street-level bureaucrats navigate policy implementation in cultural institutions
  • Discretionary power and professional strategies in arts organizations
  • Social missions and emotional labor in cultural work
  • Application of street-level bureaucracy concept across diverse global cultural policy contexts
  • Intersections between street-level bureaucracy and artistic/cultural intermediaries

Timeline

  • September 5, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Beyond the Westminster model: a myth that needs constant refreshing?
item.content:encoded:
Leighton Andrews, Cardiff University

Matthew Collins, Cardiff University

The special issue examines the relationship between ministers and civil servants within Westminster model governance systems. It addresses growing tensions between political and bureaucratic cultures, where ministers increasingly prioritize electoral cycles and party interests while civil servants maintain institutional norms of impartiality. The breakdown of traditional constitutional conventions has led to public blame attribution, demands for personal accountability of officials, and increased risk aversion among civil servants, with significant implications for policy quality and governance.

The issue invites both theoretical and empirical research exploring how the minister-official relationship affects policy-making and delivery. Contributors may focus on either side of the relationship or the relationship itself, using qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, or conceptual approaches. While emphasizing the Westminster model, comparative studies engaging with other jurisdictions and broader public administration frameworks are welcomed.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The nature and dynamics of trust between ministers and civil servants.
  • The politicization of advice and its consequences for advisory quality.
  • Risk aversion, deference, and the suppression of honesty.
  • Ethical and conduct standards.
  • The role of special advisors in mediating the minister-official relationship.
  • The consequences of ministerial turnover for policy continuity.
  • The impact of organizational or departmental culture.
  • Parliamentary accountability and the personal exposure of named officials.
  • The constitutional position of ministers and/or civil servants.
  • Historical perspectives on the cycle of strain and reform in the minister-official relationship, particularly those that reflect the impact of crises.

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Deadline for research articles
  • March 31, 2027: Deadline for debate and new development articles

item.title: Creating value for citizens in public service ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
Paula Rossi, University of Vaasa

Jim Broch Skarli, University of Inland Norway

Maria Petrescu, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University

Edwina Zhu, University of Edinburgh Business School

This special issue examines how public services can create value for citizens within public service ecosystems (PSEs), moving beyond traditional service-user and organization-centric perspectives to encompass the complex interplay of multiple actors, political contexts, and non-living elements. The PSE framework emphasizes systemic, relational, and context-dependent nature of value creation, recognizing how administrative and political governance shapes what is possible in public service environments.

The call seeks contributions that explore both societal value for communities and individual value for service users, addressing the dynamics and conditions that enable or hinder value creation across individual, organizational, and institutional levels. Submissions should advance understanding of public administration and management theory and practice, with both theoretical and empirical approaches welcome, including research articles, debate pieces, and new development articles.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Examining the implications of the roles and individual characteristics of service users in value co-creation, for example from the perspective of vulnerable service users and family carers
  • Addressing the implementation and utilization of technologies from a PSE and value creation perspective
  • Widening the empirical focus from private-benefit services to include more public-benefit services such as utility services, transportation, housing, prison management or urban development, emphasizing 'value for citizens' as an outcome
  • Exploring the implications of understanding place-based public services from a PSE and value creation perspective
  • Addressing the hindering or enabling dynamics and conditions of value creation in and between the individual, organizational and institutional levels of PSEs in particular contexts, for example by utilizing 'conflict' as an analytical tool
  • Interrogating and developing Public Service Logic (PSL) as a framework for investigating and evaluating value creation within PSEs

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Manuscript deadline for research articles and new development pieces
  • March 1, 2027: Manuscript deadline for debate pieces

item.title: From emergency response to inclusive resilient governance in an era of crises
item.content:encoded:
Paresh Wankhade, Edge Hill University Business School

Giles McClelland, Edge Hill University Business School

This special issue examines how public organizations are shifting from traditional emergency response approaches toward more inclusive and resilient governance frameworks. It addresses the complex challenges posed by modern disasters, pandemics, and crises that require coordination across professional and organizational boundaries, while emphasizing the importance of trust, legitimacy, learning, and community engagement.

The issue seeks contributions that bridge disaster management, emergency services, and public administration scholarship, with particular interest in governance capacity, collaborative networks, and the role of individual job crafting in workforce resilience. It also recognizes that crisis experiences are shaped by social inequalities, identity relations, and uneven distributions of power and resources.

Submissions may be research articles, new development pieces, or debate articles that explore topics including multi-level coordination, leadership, organizational learning, digital transformation in emergency management, and the contributions of communities and civil society to building resilience.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How are emergency services adapting to more complex, frequent and interconnected crises?
  • What forms of governance capacity are needed to manage compound and cascading risks?
  • How do public organizations co-ordinate across organizational, sectoral and jurisdictional boundaries during disasters?
  • What are the strengths and limitations of command-and-control, networked and collaborative models of emergency management?
  • How do emergency services balance centralized command with local discretion, improvisation and community knowledge?
  • How do frontline responders reshape tasks, relationships and meanings during disaster preparedness, response and recovery?
  • What forms of job crafting support workforce resilience, engagement, wellbeing and service continuity?
  • What role do leaders and managers play in influencing the job crafting behaviours of teams and individuals?
  • How do public organizations maintain trust, legitimacy and accountability during and after crises?
  • What role do identities such as women and gender-diverse actors play in community resilience, mutual aid and local crisis leadership?
  • How do inequalities shape exposure to disaster risk, access to emergency services and recovery outcomes?
  • What role do communities, civil society organizations, volunteers and private actors play in building resilience?
  • How do governments and emergency services learn or fail to learn from inquiries, reviews and past disasters?
  • How are digital technologies, data analytics, AI, early warning systems and crisis communication platforms transforming emergency management?

Timeline

  • May 1, 2027: Deadline for research articles
  • August 1, 2027: Deadline for debate and new development pieces

item.title: Populism and Public Management
item.content:encoded:
Zoe Radnor, Aston University

David Walker, Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust

This special issue examines the intersection of populism and public management, inviting cross-disciplinary perspectives from law, social sciences, politics and public administration. The rise of populist movements worldwide, spanning both left and right of the political spectrum, raises fundamental questions about how public managers and administrators navigate their responsibilities when faced with politicians whose values may conflict with liberal democratic principles and established governance standards.

The issue seeks contributions that explore critical tensions in public administration under populism: whether public managers have ethical obligations to defend democratic institutions, how they balance political responsiveness with professional integrity, and whether existing accountability frameworks adequately address challenges posed by populist policies. Contributors are encouraged to consider international comparisons and examine how different governmental structures and civil service frameworks respond to populist pressures.

Appel publié par Public Money & Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Are we facing the limits of traditional thinking in public management? Do public managers have a 'moral personality' with value commitment to liberal democracy and/or state continuity?
  • Does populism create a challenge for public managers to abide by good governance principles?
  • Are public managers obliged to defend the state from attack, rhetorical or actual?
  • Have public managers traditionally lacked 'voice' within the political–administrative interface and what challenges do they face with the rise of populism?
  • Is there a problem facing public managers if they are becoming answerable to politicians with antagonistic value sets or who may break the law?
  • How anachronistic are Weberian doctrines of 'responsiveness' in the face of populism?
  • What is 'extremism'/populism and can it be defined ex ante?
  • Do public managers observe/answer to a code that protects them against orders?
  • How far do existing doctrines of accountability accommodate answerability for extremist policies?
  • Do public managers have ethical commitments that equip them to resist political directives that might subvert constitutional order?
  • What lessons could public managers learn from international and comparative perspectives on populism?
  • Is the UK a special case with its uncodified constitutional system?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline for research articles and new development pieces
  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline for debate pieces
